title: Drishyam 3 Has Crossed ₹225 Crore Worldwide. The Overseas Numbers Tell a Story About Who's Really Watching Malayalam Cinema.
excerpt: Jeethu Joseph's franchise finale has earned more from international markets than from India — a first for a Malayalam film of this scale, and a direct measure of the diaspora's ticket-buying power.
body:
Mohanlal's *Drishyam 3* crossed ₹225 crore at the worldwide box office in its twelfth day of release. The number is impressive. The breakdown is more interesting.

## The Overseas Paradox

Of that ₹225 crore haul, approximately ₹110 crore has come from overseas markets — the Middle East, North America, Europe, and other key territories. The India gross stands at roughly ₹116 crore. For most of the film's theatrical run, international collections have actually outpaced domestic earnings.

Read that again. A Malayalam-language film, set in Kerala, about a man hiding a crime from local police, is making more money from audiences living thousands of miles from Kerala than from audiences within India itself.

This is what the Malayalam diaspora looks like when it shows up at the box office.

## The Franchise That Changed Everything

When Jeethu Joseph released the original *Drishyam* in 2013, it became the highest-grossing Malayalam film of its time. Then came the remakes — Hindi, Telugu, Tamil, Kannada, and international adaptations that carried Georgekutty's story across language barriers. *Drishyam 2* arrived in 2021 and expanded the franchise's global footprint further.

*Drishyam 3*, billed as the final chapter, carried the weight of completing a story that audiences in at least six languages have invested in over thirteen years. Despite receiving mixed critical reception — some reviewers found the plot mechanics less tight than its predecessors — the film's commercial performance has been unequivocal.

## The Numbers in Context

The ₹225 crore global gross makes *Drishyam 3* the sixth Malayalam film to cross ₹200 crore worldwide, joining a club that includes *Lokah Chapter 1* (₹304 crore), *Empuraan* (₹267 crore), *Manjummel Boys* (₹241 crore), *Thudarum* (₹235 crore), and *Vaazha 2* (₹235 crore).

That's six Malayalam films above the ₹200 crore worldwide mark. Five years ago, even one would have been considered extraordinary. The industry isn't just growing; it's rewriting what's commercially possible for a regional language cinema with roughly 38 million native speakers.

In Kerala alone, the film has dominated screen count with over 1,782 Malayalam-language shows out of 2,454 total shows across India. The Tamil, Telugu, and Kannada dubbed versions contribute modestly — ₹12 lakh, ₹5 lakh, and ₹3 lakh respectively on Day 12 — but the film wasn't designed to be a pan-India multilingual hit. It was designed to be the definitive Malayalam blockbuster, and it has delivered on that brief.

## Why NRIs Should Pay Attention

The overseas performance of *Drishyam 3* is not just a box office statistic. It's a mirror. The film's international gross, driven primarily by Malayali communities in the Gulf, the US, and the UK, reflects the deep cultural connection that diaspora audiences maintain with their home cinema.

These aren't casual viewers. These are communities that organize group bookings, drive premiere-night events, and turn a Malayalam thriller into a communal experience in cities like Dubai, Houston, and London. The ₹110 crore overseas figure is their collective vote of confidence — in the franchise, in Mohanlal, and in the idea that a story rooted in a specific Kerala milieu can resonate with people who may not have visited Kerala in years.

## What's Left

With the second-week drop kicking in — Day 12 saw collections fall to ₹2.75-3 crore from the previous day's ₹5.35 crore — the film's trajectory is clearly slowing. Industry trackers expect it to challenge the ₹250 crore worldwide mark by the end of its full theatrical run, though overtaking *Empuraan*'s ₹267 crore record would require sustained holds through its third and fourth weeks.

The cast — Mohanlal, Meena, Siddique, Asha Sharath, Murali Gopy, Ansiba Hassan, and Esther Anil — has delivered what may be the most commercially successful finale in Indian franchise history. The story that began in 2013 has ended with ₹225 crore and counting.

Georgekutty, it turns out, was worth every rupee of the ticket.
